name: VarsBelow
doc:
**The expression mentions only points numbered below `k`.**

Structural on the expression, so it is decided by inspecting the syntax rather than by reasoning about
the configuration.
stmt:
def VarsBelow : GeoExpr n → ℕ → Prop
  | .coord p _, k => p < k
  | .const _, _ => True
  | .add a b, k => a.VarsBelow k ∧ b.VarsBelow k
  | .sub a b, k => a.VarsBelow k ∧ b.VarsBelow k
  | .mul a b, k => a.VarsBelow k ∧ b.VarsBelow k

name: varsBelow_coord
stmt:
@[simp] theorem varsBelow_coord (p : ℕ) (axis : Fin n) (k : ℕ) :
    VarsBelow (.coord p axis : GeoExpr n) k ↔ p < k

name: varsBelow_const
stmt:
@[simp] theorem varsBelow_const (c : ℝ) (k : ℕ) :
    VarsBelow (.const c : GeoExpr n) k ↔ True

name: varsBelow_add
stmt:
@[simp] theorem varsBelow_add (a b : GeoExpr n) (k : ℕ) :
    VarsBelow (.add a b) k ↔ a.VarsBelow k ∧ b.VarsBelow k

name: varsBelow_sub
stmt:
@[simp] theorem varsBelow_sub (a b : GeoExpr n) (k : ℕ) :
    VarsBelow (.sub a b) k ↔ a.VarsBelow k ∧ b.VarsBelow k

name: varsBelow_mul
stmt:
@[simp] theorem varsBelow_mul (a b : GeoExpr n) (k : ℕ) :
    VarsBelow (.mul a b) k ↔ a.VarsBelow k ∧ b.VarsBelow k

name: evalFin
doc:
**Evaluate in a configuration of exactly `k` points.**

The hypothesis `h` is what makes `pts ⟨p, h⟩` well-typed at every `coord`, which is why it is a
parameter of the definition rather than of a separate lemma.
stmt: noncomputable def evalFin {k : ℕ} (e : GeoExpr n) (h : e.VarsBelow k) (pts : Fin k → Pt n) : ℝ
proof:
match e, h with
  | .coord p axis, h => pts ⟨p, h⟩ axis
  | .const c, _ => c
  | .add a b, h => a.evalFin h.1 pts + b.evalFin h.2 pts
  | .sub a b, h => a.evalFin h.1 pts - b.evalFin h.2 pts
  | .mul a b, h => a.evalFin h.1 pts * b.evalFin h.2 pts

name: evalFin_eq_evalPts
doc:
**`evalFin` agrees with `evalPts`** when the ambient family extends the finite configuration.

This is the coherence lemma: the finite evaluator is not a different semantics, it is the same one
restricted. Stated with an explicit `ext` hypothesis because extending `Fin k → Pt n` to `ℕ → Pt n`
requires choosing values for the extra points, and the choice must not matter -- which is exactly the
content of `VarsBelow`.
stmt:
theorem evalFin_eq_evalPts {k : ℕ} (e : GeoExpr n) (h : e.VarsBelow k)
    (pts : Fin k → Pt n) (ext : ℕ → Pt n)
    (hagree : ∀ p (hp : p < k), ext p = pts ⟨p, hp⟩) :
    e.evalFin h pts = e.evalPts ext
proof:
by
  induction e with
  | coord p axis =>
      simp only [evalFin, evalPts]
      rw [hagree p h]
  | const c => rfl
  | add a b iha ihb =>
      simp only [evalFin, evalPts, varsBelow_add] at *
      rw [iha h.1, ihb h.2]
  | sub a b iha ihb =>
      simp only [evalFin, evalPts, varsBelow_sub] at *
      rw [iha h.1, ihb h.2]
  | mul a b iha ihb =>
      simp only [evalFin, evalPts, varsBelow_mul] at *
      rw [iha h.1, ihb h.2]

end GeoExpr

end Lattice.Geo

name: flatEquiv
doc:
**The layout equivalence** between "a point index and a coordinate" and "a coordinate of the
flattened vector".

Stated as a `def` rather than used inline so that the round-trip lemmas below can be proved once.
stmt: def flatEquiv (k n : ℕ) : Fin k × Fin n ≃ Fin (k * n)

name: flatten
doc:
**Flatten a configuration** of `k` points in `n` dimensions to a single real vector.

This is the operation that lets the geometric layer speak to the weight layer: after it, a constraint is
a function on `Fin (k * n) → ℝ`, which is exactly a `Lattice.Lib` vector.
stmt: noncomputable def flatten (pts : Fin k → Pt n) : Fin (k * n) → ℝ
proof: fun i => pts (flatEquiv k n |>.symm i).1 (flatEquiv k n |>.symm i).2

name: unflatten
doc: **Unflatten a vector** back into a configuration.
stmt: noncomputable def unflatten (v : Fin (k * n) → ℝ) : Fin k → Pt n
proof: fun p q => v (flatEquiv k n (p, q))

name: unflatten_flatten
doc:
**The object layer is a bijection**: unflattening a flattened configuration recovers it.

This is the "对象层已证双射" half of the reversibility requirement, for the geometric chain.
stmt: @[simp] theorem unflatten_flatten (pts : Fin k → Pt n) : unflatten (flatten pts) = pts
proof:
by
  funext p q
  unfold unflatten flatten
  simp [flatEquiv]

name: flatten_unflatten
doc:
**The object layer is a bijection**: flattening an unflattened vector recovers it.

The other half. Together with `unflatten_flatten` this makes `flatten` an equivalence, which is what
allows a statement about configurations to be transported to a statement about weights without loss.
stmt: @[simp] theorem flatten_unflatten (v : Fin (k * n) → ℝ) : flatten (unflatten v) = v
proof:
by
  funext i
  unfold flatten unflatten
  rw [Equiv.apply_symm_apply]

name: flatten_injective
doc: `flatten` is injective, as a bijection must be.
stmt: theorem flatten_injective : Function.Injective (flatten (k := k) (n := n))
proof:
by
  intro a b h
  have := congrArg unflatten h
  simpa using this

name: flatten_surjective
stmt: theorem flatten_surjective : Function.Surjective (flatten (k := k) (n := n))

name: flattenEquiv
doc:
**The configuration space is equivalent to a finite-dimensional real vector space.**

The bundled form of the two round-trip laws; useful when a theorem wants `Nonempty (A ≃ B)` rather than
the two directions.
stmt:
noncomputable def flattenEquiv : (Fin k → Pt n) ≃ (Fin (k * n) → ℝ) where
  toFun
proof:
flatten
  invFun := unflatten
  left_inv := unflatten_flatten
  right_inv := flatten_unflatten

name: flattenRepresentation
stmt:
noncomputable def flattenRepresentation (k n : ℕ) :
    Lattice.Lift.Representation (Fin k → Pt n) (Fin (k * n) → ℝ)

name: flattenRepresentation_roundtrip
doc:
**`flattenRepresentation` is not the identity**: its round trip goes through `flatten` and `unflatten`, so the
statement is about those two functions rather than reducing to `p = p`.
stmt:
theorem flattenRepresentation_roundtrip (k n : ℕ) (pts : Fin k → Pt n) :
    (flattenRepresentation k n).extract ((flattenRepresentation k n).compile pts) = pts

name: flattenRepresentation_compile_extract
doc: **... and it is genuinely two-directional**, which the round-trip obligation alone does not demand.
stmt:
theorem flattenRepresentation_compile_extract (k n : ℕ) (v : Fin (k * n) → ℝ) :
    (flattenRepresentation k n).compile ((flattenRepresentation k n).extract v) = v
proof:
flattenEquiv (k := k) (n := n) |>.apply_symm_apply v

end Lattice.Geo

name: flatEquiv_val
doc:
**`finProdFinEquiv` puts the coordinate first**: the slot for `(p, i)` is `i + n * p`.

Recorded separately because the rest of the file needs it as a rewrite rule, and because it is the one place where
the two conventions visibly differ.
stmt:
theorem flatEquiv_val (p : Fin k) (i : Fin n) :
    (flatEquiv k n (p, i)).val = i.val + n * p.val

name: flatEquiv_val_eq_seqSlot
doc:
**The two slot indices are the same number**, by commutativity. This is the step that makes the agreement a
theorem rather than a definitional equality.
stmt:
theorem flatEquiv_val_eq_seqSlot (p : Fin k) (i : Fin n) :
    (flatEquiv k n (p, i)).val = p.val * n + i.val
proof:
by
  rw [flatEquiv_val]
  exact Nat.add_comm i.val (n * p.val) |>.trans (by rw [Nat.mul_comm n p.val])

name: flatten_apply
doc:
**`flatten` puts `pts p i` in the slot for `(p, i)`.**

This is the definitional fact the agreement rests on: `flatten` reads position `p` and coordinate `i` out of the slot
that `flatEquiv` assigns to the pair.
stmt:
theorem flatten_apply (pts : Fin k → Pt n) (p : Fin k) (i : Fin n) :
    flatten pts (flatEquiv k n (p, i)) = pts p i
